meta.caveat: Upgraded from a course-level stub to real per-lesson locators (2026-10-24), using the live 28-lesson sequence at the course page above (titles and one-paragraph descriptions per lesson -- not a full teacher guide with exercises, so still a notch below hour_of_data's rigor, which was built from a real 23-screen Teacher Guide PDF). locator_url_template is null: the course page lists lessons but doesn't expose a stable per-lesson URL I could confirm, so locators render as plain text, not links, until one is verified -- don't guess a scheme (see this project's own README on that point). Lesson 1 ("Computing Needs All Voices") has no entry below; it's about representation in computing, not math or programming content, and nothing in this carrier's catalogs fits it.

alignment_log.scope: Second pass. First pass (course-level, locator "course") was built from a 2-page overview PDF alone. This pass reads the real 28-lesson sequence from bootstrapworld.org's live Fall 2026 course page and re-grounds every code against a specific lesson or lessons, adding a High School Algebra/Functions slice (F-IF, F-BF, A-CED, A-REI, F-LE) the teacher asked for after noticing piecewise functions -- named in the original overview -- had no middle-school code to land on.
alignment_log.note: Dropped entirely, now that the real lesson list is in hand: all of grades 6-8 Statistics & Probability (6.SP, 7.SP, 8.SP). The first pass marked these "partial, unverified" from Bootstrap's own alignment-page claim alone; none of the 28 lessons collects, samples, or analyzes real-world data, so this pass removes the claim rather than keep guessing in its favor. Two new middle-school Geometry codes added, both strongly grounded in named lessons that weren't visible from the overview alone: 6.G.4 (nets and surface area -- Lesson 10) and 8.G.3 (coordinate transformations -- Lesson 11). High School additions are deliberately narrow: of the ~40 codes Bootstrap's own 2019 alignment page claims across A-SSE/A-CED/A-REI/F-IF/F-BF/F-LE, only 13 have a specific lesson to point to (F-IF.1/2/7, F-BF.1, A-CED.1-3, A-REI.3/10/12, F-LE.1/2/5) -- A-SSE (entirely quadratic/exponential-series), A-REI.1/2/4 (quadratics), F-IF.3-6/8-9 (sequences, quadratic/exponential analysis), F-BF.2-4 (sequences, inverses), and F-LE.3-4 (exponential-specific) have no lesson in the sequence that touches them, so they're left out rather than padded in because the domain name sounds adjacent. CSTA 2017 coverage (12 codes) carries over from the first pass, now attached to specific lessons instead of the whole course; the two DA-cluster codes already excluded in pass one (2-DA-07/08/09, 3A-DA-11, read then as a stale carryover from Bootstrap:Data Science) are confirmed excluded now that "Simple Data Types" (Lesson 5) turns out to mean Pyret's primitive types, not external data analysis.

6.NS.5.note: "Simple Data Types" covers real-world inequalities with Pyret's Number type, which plausibly includes signed values (negative scores, position deltas), but the lesson description doesn't name this specifically.

6.NS.6.note: "Coordinates" has students play a video game to identify how coordinates describe position; "Game Design" has them use coordinates for their own game's positions -- both are this standard directly.

6.NS.7.note: "Simple Data Types" introduces real-world inequalities with ordered/signed values; "Simple Inequalities" has students identify solutions and non-solutions, which depends on ordering and absolute value.

6.NS.8.note: "Distance in Video Games" has students find distances between coordinate points, the applied form of this standard.

6.G.4.note: "Surface Area of a Rectangular Prism" has students build a paper prism from a printed net and calculate its surface area -- this standard almost verbatim.

7.EE.1.note: "Order of Operations," using Bootstrap's own "Circles of Evaluation" model, is generating and reading equivalent arithmetic expressions.

7.EE.2.note: Rewriting an expression to see how quantities relate is the same move "Function Composition" makes with image-transformation functions, though the lesson's own framing is programming, not algebraic rewriting.

7.EE.3.note: "Order of Operations" and "Solving Word Problems with the Design Recipe" (multi-step problems, checked via the Design Recipe's own verification step) both match this standard directly.

7.EE.4.note: Word problems solved via the Design Recipe (19), revenue/cost/profit problems (21, "Problem Decomposition"), and inequalities applied to keep a game character on screen (22, 24) are this standard's equation- and inequality-writing both.

8.F.1.note: "Contracts for Strings and Images," "Functions Make Life Easier!," "The Vertical Line Test," "Functions: Contracts, Examples & Definitions," and "Functions for Character Animation" are this course's core, repeated treatment of a function as a rule from input to output.

8.F.2.note: "Functions Can Be Linear" and "Defining Linear Functions" both explore slope and intercept using definitions, tables, and graphs -- comparing representations of the same function.

8.F.3.note: Same two lessons: reading y = mx + b as a linear function via slope and intercept is this standard directly.

8.G.3.note: "Transforming and Composing Images" has students scale and position shapes using coordinates -- this standard's own description of dilations and translations by coordinate.

8.G.6.note: "Distance in Video Games" says students "explore the Pythagorean Theorem," which could include why it holds, not just applying it -- not specific enough in the course page's own description to call this strong.

8.G.7.note: "Distance in Video Games" explicitly explores the Pythagorean Theorem to find unknown lengths, before extending it to the distance formula.

8.G.8.note: "Distance in Video Games" and "Collision Detection" are built around applying the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two coordinate points -- the strongest single match in this carrier, and the concept the original course overview names by name.

F-IF.1.note: "Function Notation" has students read f(x) notation and evaluate it via definitions, tables, and graphs -- this standard directly, at a level middle school's 8.F.1 explicitly excludes ("function notation isn't required in Grade 8").

F-IF.2.note: Same lesson: evaluating functions at given inputs and interpreting function-notation statements in context.

F-IF.7.note: "Piecewise Functions and Conditionals" and "Player Animation" (piecewise functions for movement by keypress) are this standard's own piecewise/step-function clause, named explicitly in the original course overview as taught content.

F-BF.1.note: "Function Composition," the nested compositions in "Function Notation" (f(g(h(x)))), and "Collision Detection" (combining function composition with distance and inequality) are this standard's own compose-functions clause.

A-CED.1.note: "Solving Word Problems with the Design Recipe" writes one-variable equations from word problems -- this standard directly.

A-CED.2.note: The linear-function lessons write and graph two-variable equations (y = mx + b) on labeled axes.

A-CED.3.note: The video-game project, compound inequalities, and collision detection all use inequalities or systems of them to represent a constraint (staying on screen, detecting a collision) and judge whether a value satisfies it.

A-REI.3.note: Solving one-variable linear equations (19) and identifying solutions/non-solutions of one-variable inequalities (22) are this standard directly.

A-REI.10.note: Graphing linear functions as the set of (x, y) pairs satisfying y = mx + b is this standard's own definition of a two-variable equation's graph.

A-REI.12.note: "Simple Inequalities," "Compound Inequalities" (union and intersection), and "Sam the Butterfly" (keeping a character on screen) are this standard's half-plane and system-of-inequalities graphing.

F-LE.1.note: The linear-function lessons teach recognizing a constant-rate (linear) relationship, this standard's part (b); nothing in the course distinguishes linear from exponential growth, part (a)/(c), so this is a partial match to one part of a three-part standard.

F-LE.2.note: Building a linear function from a table, graph, or two points is exactly what these two lessons teach.

F-LE.5.note: Interpreting slope and intercept in context (a per-unit rate, a starting value) runs through the linear-function lessons, the Design Recipe word problems, and the revenue/cost/profit problem decomposition.

2-AP-11.note: Naming variables clearly runs through "Game Design," "Simple Data Types," and especially "Defining Values," which is this standard by name.

2-AP-13.note: "Problem Decomposition" is this standard's own name; "Game Design" also has students break a game concept into pieces before building it.

2-AP-14.note: "Function Composition" generalizes repeated image-transformation steps into reusable functions -- this standard's own parameterization idea.

2-AP-17.note: The video-game project and collision detection both require testing a program (does the character correctly stay on screen, is a collision correctly detected) against cases designed to find bugs.

2-AP-19.note: "Contracts for Strings and Images" and "Functions: Contracts, Examples & Definitions" both teach documenting a function's name, domain, and range so someone else can use it correctly.

3A-AP-16.note: Character animation, keeping a character on screen by keypress, and piecewise player movement by keypress are all events triggering a procedure -- this standard's own definition of reactive programming.

3A-AP-17.note: "Problem Decomposition," at this course's upper grade band, breaking revenue/cost/profit into separate, reusable functions.

3A-AP-18.note: The full video-game project (player, danger, target, multiple functions working together) is plausibly a system of interacting pieces, but the course page's own description doesn't detail its architecture enough to confirm this specifically.

3A-AP-23.note: Function contracts, examples, and definitions are exactly this standard's documentation of a design decision, so another student (or the original one, later) can follow it.

3B-AP-14.note: Building one's own game components rather than only using provided ones runs through the project lessons -- the course overview's own framing is that students "program a videogame of their own design."

3B-AP-21.note: The Design Recipe (word problems solved by writing test cases before the function body) and collision detection (verifying detection logic against its own spec) are this standard's own test-case-first practice, and match Bootstrap's own publicly documented pedagogy.

3B-AP-22.note: Adding collision detection to an already-working game (28) risks breaking existing behavior, a real but not explicitly named risk in the course page's own description.
